pumac-2019-power-01a.title: Additivity
pumac-2019-power-01a.body: The events $A$ and $A^c=\Omega\setminus A$ are disjoint and $A\cup A^c=\Omega$. By additivity, $P(A)+P(A^c)=P(A\cup A^c)=P(\Omega)=1$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-01b.title: Split $B$
pumac-2019-power-01b.body: Since $A\subseteq B$, $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$ with the two pieces disjoint. Hence $P(B)=P(A)+P(B\setminus A)\ge P(A)$ because probabilities are nonnegative. ∎

pumac-2019-power-02b.title: Sum of nonnegative terms
pumac-2019-power-02b.body:
Let $\mu=E(X)$. $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\sum_t(t-\mu)^2P(X=t)$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is $0$ iff each term is $0$, i.e. iff $P(X=t)=0$ for every $t\ne\mu$, i.e. iff $P(X=\mu)=1$.

Conversely if $X=c$ with probability $1$ then $\mu=c$ and the sum is $0$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-02d.title: Use independence
pumac-2019-power-02d.body:
For independent $X,Y$: $E(XY)=\sum_{x,y}xyP(X=x)P(Y=y)=E(X)E(Y)$. By part (3),
$$\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=E(X^2)+2E(XY)+E(Y^2)-(E(X)+E(Y))^2=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2\big(E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)\big),$$
and the last bracket is $0$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-03.title: Induction
pumac-2019-power-03.body:
For two events, $A_1\cup A_2=A_1\cup(A_2\setminus A_1)$ is a disjoint union, so $P(A_1\cup A_2)=P(A_1)+P(A_2\setminus A_1)\le P(A_1)+P(A_2)$ (using monotonicity from Problem 1.4.1).

Assume the claim for $n-1$ events. Then
$$P(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_n)\le P(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_{n-1})+P(A_n)\le\sum_{i=1}^nP(A_i).$$ ∎

pumac-2019-power-04.title: Markov
pumac-2019-power-04.body:
$$E(X)=\sum_x xP(X=x)\ge\sum_{x\ge t}xP(X=x)\ge t\sum_{x\ge t}P(X=x)=tP(X\ge t),$$
where the first inequality drops the nonnegative terms with $x<t$ (here $X\ge0$ is used). Divide by $t$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-05c.title: Linearity
pumac-2019-power-05c.body:
Each roll has expectation $7/2$, so the sum has expectation $100\cdot\frac72=350$.

**Answer: 350**

pumac-2019-power-05d.title: Variances add
pumac-2019-power-05d.body:
The rolls are independent, so variances add (Problem 1.4.2(4)): $100\cdot\frac{35}{12}=\frac{875}{3}$.

**Answer: $875/3$**

pumac-2019-power-06a.title: First-step analysis
pumac-2019-power-06a.body:
Let $E=E(R)$. Draw a card: with probability $\frac12$ it is black and we start over after 1 draw: $1+E$. With probability $\frac12$ it is red; then let $F$ be the remaining expectation given the last card is red: next card red (prob. $\frac12$) finishes after 1 more draw, black restarts: $F=1+\frac12\cdot0+\frac12E$. So $E=1+\frac12E+\frac12F$ with $F=1+\frac12E$, giving $E=1+\frac12E+\frac12+\frac14E$, i.e. $\frac14E=\frac32$ and $E=6$.

**Answer: 6**

pumac-2019-power-06b.title: First-step analysis
pumac-2019-power-06b.body:
Let $a$ be the expectation from the start and $b$ the expectation when the last card is red. Then $a=1+\frac12b+\frac12a$ and $b=1+\frac12\cdot0+\frac12b$ (another red keeps us in the 'last card red' state, black finishes). So $b=2$ and $\frac12a=1+1$, $a=4$.

**Answer: 4**

pumac-2019-power-06c.title: First-step analysis
pumac-2019-power-06c.body:
Let $E=E(K)$ and $F$ the expectation given the last card is a red king. $E=1+pF+(1-p)E$ and $F=1+(1-p)E$ (success with probability $p$ ends the process). Then $pE=1+pF$ , $F=1+(1-p)E$ gives $pE=1+p+p(1-p)E$, so $p^2E=1+p$, $E=\frac1p+\frac1{p^2}=26+676=702$.

**Answer: 702**

pumac-2019-power-06d.title: Identify $M$
pumac-2019-power-06d.body:
The process stops at the first moment a red card is followed by any card (RR gives $R$, RB gives $B$). So $M=1+T$, where $T$ is the index of the first red card. $T$ is geometric with success probability $\frac12$, so $E(T)=2$ and $E(M)=3$.

**Answer: 3**

pumac-2019-power-08a.title: Condition on the first coin
pumac-2019-power-08a.body:
Given the first toss is heads, the first coin is the two-headed coin with probability $\frac{1/3}{1/2}=\frac23$ and the fair coin with probability $\frac13$ (the two-tailed coin is impossible).

- If it was two-headed, the second coin is fair or two-tailed (each prob. $\frac12$): $P(H)=\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$.
- If it was fair, the second coin is two-headed or two-tailed: $P(H)=\frac12$.

Total: $\frac23\cdot\frac14+\frac13\cdot\frac12=\frac16+\frac16=\frac13$.

**Answer: $1/3$**

pumac-2019-power-08b.title: Independence
pumac-2019-power-08b.body:
The second draw and toss are independent of the first, and a random coin shows heads with probability $\frac13(\frac12+1+0)=\frac12$.

**Answer: $1/2$**

pumac-2019-power-09.title: Random dilation modulo a prime
pumac-2019-power-09.body:
Choose a prime $p=3k+2$ larger than $2\max|s|$ (there are infinitely many primes $\equiv2\pmod 3$). Then no $s\in S$ is $\equiv0\pmod p$. Let $T=\{k+1,\dots,2k+1\}\subset\mathbb Z_p$, $|T|=k+1$.

**$T$ is sum-free mod $p$:** $T+T\subseteq\{2k+2,\dots,4k+2\}$; reducing mod $p=3k+2$ this is $\{2k+2,\dots,3k+1\}\cup\{0,\dots,k\}$, disjoint from $T$.

Pick $x\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$ uniformly and set $X_x=\{s\in S:\ xs\bmod p\in T\}$. If $a,b,a+b\in X_x$, then $xa,xb,x(a+b)=xa+xb\in T$, contradicting sum-freeness; so $X_x$ is sum-free.

For fixed $s\in S$, $xs$ is uniform on the nonzero residues, so $P(s\in X_x)=\frac{k+1}{3k+1}>\frac13$. By linearity of expectation $E|X_x|>\frac13|S|$, so some $x$ gives $|X_x|\ge\frac13|S|$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-10.title: Linearity of expectation
pumac-2019-power-10.body:
There are $\binom n3$ triples of vertices; each forms a triangle exactly when its three edges are all chosen, which has probability $p^3$. By linearity of expectation the expected number is $\binom n3p^3$.

**Answer: $\binom n3p^3$**

pumac-2019-power-11.title: Probabilistic construction
pumac-2019-power-11.body:
If $4\le n<32$, take the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$: it has $n^2<32n$ edges and clearly works.

Let $n\ge32$, $k=\lfloor n/4\rfloor\ge\frac{29}{32}\cdot\frac n4$. Choose $31n$ edges independently and uniformly at random from $A\times B$ (repetition allowed); the resulting graph has at most $31n<32n$ edges.

Fix $X\subseteq A$, $Y\subseteq B$ with $|X|=|Y|=k$. Each chosen edge lies in $X\times Y$ with probability $\frac{k^2}{n^2}\ge\left(\frac{29}{128}\right)^2>0.05$, so
$$P(\text{no edge in }X\times Y)\le(0.95)^{31n}<e^{-1.5n}\ (\text{since }31\ln\tfrac1{0.95}>1.58).$$
The number of pairs $(X,Y)$ is $\binom nk^2\le\left(2^{H(1/4)n}\right)^2<2^{1.63n}<e^{1.13n}$ ($H$ the binary entropy, $H(1/4)<0.82$). By the union bound the probability that some pair has no edge is at most $e^{1.13n-1.5n}<1$. Hence a suitable graph exists. ∎

pumac-2019-power-12a.title: From part (b)
pumac-2019-power-12a.body: By part (b) (proved in the next question) $P((U,W)\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-regular})\to1$ as $m\to\infty$, so it exceeds $\frac12$ for all sufficiently large $m$, in particular for infinitely many. ∎

pumac-2019-power-12b.title: Concentration and a union bound
pumac-2019-power-12b.body:
For fixed $X\subseteq U,Y\subseteq W$ with $|X|,|Y|\ge\varepsilon m$, $e(X,Y)$ is a sum of $|X||Y|$ independent indicator variables of mean $p$. By Hoeffding's inequality,
$$P\big(|d(X,Y)-p|>\tfrac\varepsilon2\big)\le2\exp\!\big(-2(\tfrac\varepsilon2)^2|X||Y|\big)\le2\exp(-\tfrac12\varepsilon^4m^2).$$
There are at most $2^m\cdot2^m=4^m$ pairs $(X,Y)$ (including $(U,W)$ itself). So with probability at least $1-4^m\cdot2e^{-\varepsilon^4m^2/2}\to1$, every such pair satisfies $|d(X,Y)-p|\le\frac\varepsilon2$. Then for all large $X,Y$: $|d(X,Y)-d(U,W)|\le|d(X,Y)-p|+|p-d(U,W)|\le\varepsilon$, i.e. $(U,W)$ is $\varepsilon$-regular. Since $4^m\cdot2e^{-\varepsilon^4m^2/2}\to0$, the claim follows. ∎

pumac-2019-power-13.title: Bound each term
pumac-2019-power-13.body: Each $q(U,W)\ge0$ gives $q(P)\ge0$. Since $d(U,W)^2\le1$, $q(P)\le\frac1{n^2}\sum_{\{U,W\}}|U||W|$. The sum counts pairs of vertices lying in different parts, so it is at most $\binom n2<\frac{n^2}{2}$. Hence $q(P)\le\frac12$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-14.title: Apply the lemma pairwise
pumac-2019-power-14.body:
For distinct parts $U,W$ of $P$ let $\mathcal U,\mathcal W$ be the parts of $P'$ contained in $U$ resp. $W$ (they partition $U$, $W$). Every pair of distinct parts of $P'$ lying in different parts of $P$ arises exactly once as $(u,w)\in\mathcal U\times\mathcal W$ for a unique pair $\{U,W\}$. Hence
$$q(P')=\sum_{\{U,W\}}q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)+\sum_{\text{pairs inside a part of }P}q(\cdot,\cdot)\ \ge\ \sum_{\{U,W\}}q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)\ \ge\ \sum_{\{U,W\}}q(U,W)=q(P),$$
using nonnegativity of the second sum and the lemma. ∎

**Lemma used (from the text).** For $(u,w)$ uniform in $U\times W$ let $Z=d(U',W')$ where $u\in U'\in\mathcal U$, $w\in W'\in\mathcal W$. Then $E(Z)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}\frac{e(U',W')}{|U'||W'|}=d(U,W)$ and $E(Z^2)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}d(U',W')^2=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}\big(q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)-q(U,W)\big)\ge0$.

pumac-2019-power-15.title: Variance of $Z$
pumac-2019-power-15.body:
Since $(U,W)$ is not $\varepsilon$-regular there are $U_1\subseteq U$, $W_1\subseteq W$ with $|U_1|\ge\varepsilon|U|$, $|W_1|\ge\varepsilon|W|$ and $|d(U_1,W_1)-d(U,W)|>\varepsilon$. Let $Z$ be as in the lemma for the partitions $\mathcal U,\mathcal W$. With probability $\frac{|U_1||W_1|}{|U||W|}\ge\varepsilon^2$ the point $(u,w)$ lies in $U_1\times W_1$, where $Z=d(U_1,W_1)$ deviates from $E(Z)=d(U,W)$ by more than $\varepsilon$. Therefore $\mathrm{Var}(Z)\ge\varepsilon^2\cdot\varepsilon^2=\varepsilon^4$, and by the lemma $\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}(q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)-q(U,W))\ge\varepsilon^4$. ∎

**Lemma used (from the text).** For $(u,w)$ uniform in $U\times W$ let $Z=d(U',W')$ where $u\in U'\in\mathcal U$, $w\in W'\in\mathcal W$. Then $E(Z)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}\frac{e(U',W')}{|U'||W'|}=d(U,W)$ and $E(Z^2)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}d(U',W')^2=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}\big(q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)-q(U,W)\big)\ge0$.

pumac-2019-power-16.title: Construction and index gain
pumac-2019-power-16.body:
Let $c=|V_i|$; then $kc\le n$ and $kc\ge(1-\varepsilon)n\ge\frac34n$.

**Refine.** Since $|V_0|\le\varepsilon n$ and $P$ is not $\varepsilon$-regular, more than $\varepsilon k^2$ pairs $(V_i,V_j)$ are not $\varepsilon$-regular. For each such pair, Problem 2.1.4 gives a split of $V_i$ into $\le2$ sets and of $V_j$ into $\le2$ sets; for $\varepsilon$-regular pairs use the trivial splits. For each $i$, let $\mathcal A_i$ be the common refinement of the $k-1$ splits of $V_i$ (one for each $j\neq i$): at most $2^{k-1}$ atoms. Let $P''$ be the partition into all atoms (with $V_0$ as singletons).

**Equalize.** Let $b=\lceil c/4^k\rceil$. Cut each atom into disjoint blocks of size $b$ and move the remainder (fewer than $b$ vertices, so at most $c/4^k$) of each atom into the exceptional set. At most $k\cdot2^{k-1}\cdot\frac{c}{4^k}\le\frac{n}{2^{k+1}}$ vertices are moved, so $|V_0'|\le|V_0|+\frac n{2^k}$. All blocks have size $b$, so $P'$ is equitable. Each $V_i$ yields at most $c/b\le4^k$ blocks, so $l\le k4^k$, and $l\ge k$ since each $V_i$ has at least one block. $P'$ refines $P''$ (moving vertices to $V_0$ and cutting into blocks are refinements), which refines $P$.

**Index.** By Problem 2.1.3, $q(P')\ge q(P'')$. In $P''$, consider the pair of the parts $V_i,V_j$ of $P$: the atoms in $V_i$ and $V_j$ refine the splits of Problem 2.1.4, so by the lemma applied to the further refinement and by 2.1.4, the contribution of $(V_i,V_j)$ is at least $q(V_i,V_j)+\frac{c^2}{n^2}\varepsilon^4$ if the pair is irregular, and at least $q(V_i,V_j)$ otherwise. Pairs involving $V_0$ are unchanged and pairs inside one part add something $\ge0$. Hence
$$q(P')\ge q(P)+\varepsilon k^2\cdot\frac{c^2}{n^2}\varepsilon^4\ge q(P)+\varepsilon^5\cdot\frac9{16}\ge q(P)+\frac12\varepsilon^5,$$
using $kc\ge\frac34n$. ∎

**Lemma used (from the text).** For $(u,w)$ uniform in $U\times W$ let $Z=d(U',W')$ where $u\in U'\in\mathcal U$, $w\in W'\in\mathcal W$. Then $E(Z)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}\frac{e(U',W')}{|U'||W'|}=d(U,W)$ and $E(Z^2)=\sum\frac{|U'||W'|}{|U||W|}d(U',W')^2=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{n^2}{|U||W|}\big(q(\mathcal U,\mathcal W)-q(U,W)\big)\ge0$.

pumac-2019-power-17.title: Iterate the refinement
pumac-2019-power-17.body:
**Reductions.** An $\varepsilon'$-regular partition is $\varepsilon$-regular for $\varepsilon'\le\varepsilon$, and having $k\ge t'$ parts gives $k\ge t$ for $t'\ge t$; so we may assume $\varepsilon<\frac14$ and $2^{t-2}>\varepsilon^{-6}$.

**Start.** Let $n\ge T=k_s$. Split $V$ into $t$ equal parts and put the $<t$ leftover vertices into $V_0$: $|V_0|<t\le\frac\varepsilon2n$ since $n\ge k_s\ge t4^t\ge\frac{2t}{\varepsilon}$ (as $4^t>2/\varepsilon$).

**Iterate.** While the current partition $P_i$ (equitable, $k$ parts, $|V_0|\le\varepsilon n$) is not $\varepsilon$-regular, apply Problem 2.1.5 to get $P_{i+1}$ with $q(P_{i+1})\ge q(P_i)+\frac12\varepsilon^5$, at most $k4^k$ parts, and exceptional set larger by at most $n/2^{k}$. Since $0\le q\le\frac12$ (Problem 2.1.2), after $i$ steps $\frac i2\varepsilon^5\le\frac12$, so at most $s=\lceil\varepsilon^{-5}\rceil$ steps occur. The numbers of parts satisfy $k^{(i)}\le k_i$ (as $x\mapsto x4^x$ is increasing), and $k^{(i)}\ge t$.

**Exceptional set.** The parts count at step $i$ is $\ge t$, so the total added to $V_0$ is at most $\sum_{i<s}n/2^{k_i}\le sn/2^t\le\frac{2}{\varepsilon^5}\cdot\frac{\varepsilon^6}{4}n=\frac\varepsilon2n$. With the initial $|V_0|<\frac\varepsilon2n$ we get $|V_0|\le\varepsilon n$ throughout (so 2.1.5 applies at every step).

The process ends with an $\varepsilon$-regular partition having between $t$ and $k_s=T$ parts. ∎

pumac-2019-power-18.title: Regularity cleaning and counting
pumac-2019-power-18.body:
We may assume $\varepsilon\le1$. Put $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon/10$, $t=\lceil10/\varepsilon\rceil$ and $T=T(\varepsilon_1,t)$. If $n<T$, take $\delta\le T^{-3}$: $G$ has at least one triangle (it is $\varepsilon$-far, so not triangle-free) and $\delta n^3<1$. So let $n\ge T$ and take an $\varepsilon_1$-regular partition $V_0,\dots,V_k$, $t\le k\le T$, $c=|V_i|\le n/k$.

**Remove** (i) all edges meeting $V_0$: $\le\varepsilon_1n\cdot n=\frac\varepsilon{10}n^2$; (ii) edges inside the $V_i$: $\le k\binom c2\le\frac{n^2}{2k}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{20}n^2$; (iii) edges in the $\le\varepsilon_1k^2$ irregular pairs: $\le\varepsilon_1k^2c^2\le\frac\varepsilon{10}n^2$; (iv) edges in pairs of density $<\frac{3\varepsilon}{10}$: $\le\binom k2\frac{3\varepsilon}{10}c^2\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{20}n^2$. In total $\le0.4\varepsilon n^2<\varepsilon n^2$, so a triangle survives. Its vertices lie in three distinct parts, say $V_1,V_2,V_3$, and all three pairs are $\varepsilon_1$-regular with densities $d_{12},d_{13},d_{23}\ge3\varepsilon_1$.

**Count.** All but fewer than $\varepsilon_1c$ vertices $v\in V_1$ have $|N(v)\cap V_2|\ge(d_{12}-\varepsilon_1)c\ge2\varepsilon_1c$ (otherwise the exceptional vertices $X$ with $|X|\ge\varepsilon_1 c$ would give $d(X,V_2)<d_{12}-\varepsilon_1$); likewise for $V_3$. So at least $(1-2\varepsilon_1)c\ge c/2$ vertices $v\in V_1$ have both $|N(v)\cap V_2|\ge2\varepsilon_1c$ and $|N(v)\cap V_3|\ge2\varepsilon_1c$. For such $v$, regularity of $(V_2,V_3)$ gives $d(N(v)\cap V_2,N(v)\cap V_3)\ge d_{23}-\varepsilon_1\ge2\varepsilon_1$, hence at least $2\varepsilon_1(2\varepsilon_1c)^2=8\varepsilon_1^3c^2$ edges between the two neighbourhoods, i.e. $v$ lies in at least $8\varepsilon_1^3c^2$ triangles with vertices in $V_1,V_2,V_3$. Thus there are at least $\frac c2\cdot8\varepsilon_1^3c^2=4\varepsilon_1^3c^3$ triangles. Since $c\ge\frac{(1-\varepsilon_1)n}{k}\ge\frac{3n}{4T}$, the count is at least $4\varepsilon_1^3\big(\frac3{4T}\big)^3n^3=:\delta n^3$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-19.title: Triangle removal and 3-term progressions
pumac-2019-power-19.body:
**Bob wins**: whatever $p$ Alice picks, Bob chooses $N$ large (in terms of $p$). Then $|Y|\ge(1-p)N$. We show $Y$ contains a 3-term arithmetic progression $a,c,b$ with $a+b=2c$ and $a,b,c$ distinct.

Build a tripartite graph with classes $V_1=[N]$, $V_2=[2N]$, $V_3=[3N]$ (disjoint copies, $6N$ vertices). For $x\in V_1,y\in V_2,z\in V_3$: join $x\sim y$ if $y-x\in Y$, $y\sim z$ if $z-y\in Y$, and $x\sim z$ if $z-x\in2Y$.

For each $h\in[N]$ and $a\in Y$ there is the triangle $T_{h,a}=(h,h+a,h+2a)$ (indeed $h+a\le2N$, $h+2a\le3N$). These $N|Y|$ triangles are pairwise edge-disjoint: any two of the three vertices of $T_{h,a}$ determine $a$ and $h$. Hence at least $N|Y|\ge(1-p)N^2=\frac{1-p}{36}(6N)^2$ edges must be removed to destroy all triangles. By the Coupon theorem the graph has $\ge\delta(6N)^3>N^2\ge N|Y|$ triangles when $N$ is large, so there is a triangle $(x,y,z)$ other than the $T_{h,a}$. Put $a=y-x$, $b=z-y$ (both in $Y$) and $z-x=2c$ with $c\in Y$, so $a+b=2c$. If $a=b$ then $c=a$ and the triangle is $T_{x,a}$, a contradiction. So $a\ne b$, hence $c=\frac{a+b}2$ differs from both $a$ and $b$: three distinct elements of $Y$ one of which is the mean of the other two. Bob wins. ∎

**Answer: Bob**

pumac-2019-power-20.title: Digits on a sphere
pumac-2019-power-20.body:
Fix an integer $s>4/p$. Let $N$ be large, $D=\lfloor N^{1/s}/2\rfloor$ and $B=2D$, so $B^s\le N$. Consider the integers $x=\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}x_iB^i$ with digits $0\le x_i\le D-1$: there are $D^s$ of them. For such $x,y$ the sum $x+y$ has digits $x_i+y_i\le2D-2<B$, so there are no carries.

The value $r=\sum x_i^2$ takes at most $s(D-1)^2+1\le sD^2$ values, so some class $A_r=\{x:\sum x_i^2=r\}$ has $|A_r|\ge D^s/(sD^2)$.

**No progressions.** Suppose $a,b,c\in A_r$ with $a+b=2c$. Without carries this holds digitwise: $a_i+b_i=2c_i$. As vectors in $\mathbb R^s$: $|a-b|^2=2|a|^2+2|b|^2-|a+b|^2=4r-4|c|^2=0$, so $a=b$ and hence $a=b=c$. Thus $A_r$ contains no three distinct numbers one of which is the mean of the other two.

**Size.** Let $Y=A_r+1\subseteq[1,B^s]\subseteq[1,N]$ (translation preserves the property). For $N$ large ($N^{1/s}\ge4$, so $D\ge N^{1/s}/4$): $|Y|\ge\frac{D^{s-2}}{s}\ge\frac{N^{1-2/s}}{4^{s-2}s}>N^{1-p}$ as soon as $N^{p-2/s}>4^{s-2}s$, which holds for large $N$ because $p-\frac2s>\frac p2>0$. $Y\ne X$ because $1,2,3\in X$ but not all in $Y$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-21.title: Averaging
pumac-2019-power-21.body: For $a,a'\in A$ we have $a'=(x,y)-a\in A\cap A_{x,y}$ iff $(x,y)=a+a'$ (so $a'\in A_{x,y}$ because $a'=(x,y)-a$). So $\sum_{(x,y)}|A\cap A_{x,y}|=|A|^2$, the sum over the $(2n-1)^2<(2n)^2$ possible values $(x,y)\in\{2,\dots,2n\}^2$ of $a+a'$ (other shifts give $0$). Hence some $(x,y)$ has $|A\cap A_{x,y}|\ge\frac{|A|^2}{(2n-1)^2}\ge\frac{|A|^2}{(2n)^2}$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-22a.title: Corners from triangle removal
pumac-2019-power-22a.body:
By Problem 2.2.4 there is $(x_0,y_0)$ with $B=A\cap A_{x_0,y_0}$ of size $\ge\frac{|A|^2}{4n^2}\ge\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}n^2$. $B\subseteq A$ and $B$ is symmetric under the point reflection $\rho:p\mapsto(x_0,y_0)-p$.

**Graph.** Vertex classes: $V_1$ = vertical lines $x=i$ ($i\in[n]$), $V_2$ = horizontal lines $y=j$ ($j\in[n]$), $V_3$ = lines $x+y=m$ ($m\in[2,2n]$). So at most $4n$ vertices. Two lines from different classes are adjacent iff their intersection point lies in $B$.

Each $b\in B$ gives the triangle formed by the three lines through $b$; these $|B|$ triangles are edge-disjoint (an edge determines its intersection point). So at least $|B|\ge\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4}n^2\ge\frac{\varepsilon^2}{64}(4n)^2$ edges must be removed; the graph has $N'=4n-1\ge3n$ vertices and $|B|\ge\frac{\varepsilon^2}{64}N'^2$, so by the Coupon theorem (with $\varepsilon^2/64$) there are $\ge\delta(3n)^3>n^2\ge|B|$ triangles for $n$ large. Take a triangle not coming from a point of $B$: lines $x=i$, $y=j$, $x+y=m$ with $m\ne i+j$ and $(i,j),(i,m-i),(m-j,j)\in B$. With $d=m-i-j\ne0$ these are $(i,j),(i,j+d),(i+d,j)$.

If $d>0$ this is a corner in $B\subseteq A$. If $d<0$, apply $\rho$: $\rho$ maps $B$ to itself and sends the three points to $(x_0-i,y_0-j)$, $(x_0-i,y_0-j+|d|)$, $(x_0-i+|d|,y_0-j)$, a corner with $d'=|d|>0$ in $B\subseteq A$ (all coordinates are positive, being points of $B$). ∎

pumac-2019-power-22b.title: Pass to a residue class
pumac-2019-power-22b.body: Split $[n]^2$ into the $6$ classes by $(x\bmod3,\,y\bmod2)$. Some class $(r,s)$ contains at least $\frac{\varepsilon}6n^2$ points of $A$. Write its points as $(3i+r,\,2j+s)$ and map them to $(i',j')=(i+1,j+1)$; the image $A'$ lies in a square $[m]^2$ with $m=\lceil n/2\rceil$ and has density $\ge\frac{\varepsilon}{6}$ (indeed $|A'|\ge\frac\varepsilon6n^2\ge\frac\varepsilon6m^2$). For $n$ large, Part (a) gives a corner $(i,j),(i,j+d),(i+d,j)\in A'$. Mapping back gives the points $(3i+r,2j+s)$, $(3i+r,2j+s+2d)$, $(3i+r+3d,2j+s)$ of $A$ (writing $x=3i+r$, $y=2j+s$): $(x,y),(x,y+2d),(x+3d,y)$. So the answer is **Yes**. ∎

pumac-2019-power-22c.title: Pass to a residue class
pumac-2019-power-22c.body: Split $[n]^2$ by $(x\bmod4,\,y\bmod2)$ into $8$ classes; some class $(r,s)$ contains $\ge\frac\varepsilon8n^2$ points of $A$. Its points are $(4i+r,2j+s)$; map them to $(i+1,j+1)$, which lies in $[m]^2$ with $m=\lceil n/2\rceil$ and has density $\ge\varepsilon/8$. A corner $(i,j),(i,j+d),(i+d,j)$ of the image (Part (a), $n$ large) maps back to $(x,y),(x,y+2d),(x+4d,y)$ with $x=4i+r$, $y=2j+s$. So the answer is **Yes**. ∎

pumac-2019-power-23.title: Ruzsa–Szemerédi graph
pumac-2019-power-23.body:
**The claim is true.** Let $n$ be large, $N$ a prime with $4039n<N\le8078n$ (Bertrand). View $X\subseteq[n]\subseteq\mathbb Z_N$. Take three copies $V_1,V_2,V_3$ of $\mathbb Z_N$ and define, for $x\in V_1,y\in V_2,z\in V_3$:
- $y\sim z$ iff $a(y,z)=4039y+2020z\in X$,
- $x\sim z$ iff $b(x,z)=4039x-2019z\in X$,
- $x\sim y$ iff $c(x,y)=2020x+2019y\in X$.

One checks $2019a+2020b-4039c=0$ identically in $(x,y,z)$ (coefficient of $x$: $2020\cdot4039-4039\cdot2020$; of $y$: $2019\cdot4039-4039\cdot2019$; of $z$: $2019\cdot2020-2020\cdot2019$). So every triangle gives $a,b,c\in X$ with $2019a+2020b\equiv4039c\pmod N$; as $|2019a+2020b-4039c|<4039n<N$, the equation holds over $\mathbb Z$.

**Trivial triangles.** For $m\in X$ and $x\in\mathbb Z_N$ put $y=(m-2020x)/2019$, $z=(4039x-m)/2019$ (mod $N$); then $a=b=c=m$. These $N|X|$ triangles are edge-disjoint: an edge $(y,z)$ fixes $m=a$ and then $x$ (from $c=m$); similarly for the other edge types. So at least $N|X|\ge\varepsilon nN\ge\frac{\varepsilon}{8078\cdot9}(3N)^2$ edges must be removed to destroy all triangles. By the Coupon theorem there are $\ge\delta(3N)^3>N^2\ge N|X|$ triangles for $n$ large, so some triangle is not trivial.

Such a triangle gives $a,b,c\in X$, not all equal (if $a=b=c=m$ the triangle is one of the trivial ones, since $m$ and $x$ determine $y,z$), with $2019(a-c)=-2020(b-c)$. As $\gcd(2019,2020)=1$: $a-c=2020t$, $b-c=-2019t$ with $t\ne0$. Then $a\ne c$, $b\ne c$ and $a-b=4039t\ne0$: distinct. ∎

pumac-2019-power-24.title: Greedy embedding in a dense regular triple
pumac-2019-power-24.body:
Run the cleaning argument of the Coupon theorem with regularity parameter $\eta\le\varepsilon/10$ (and $t=\lceil10/\varepsilon\rceil$): it yields parts $V_1,V_2,V_3$ of size $c\ge\frac{3n}{4T}$ ($T=T(\eta,t)$) with all pairs $\eta$-regular of density $\ge d_0:=3\varepsilon/10$. Note $\eta<d_0/2$. We also take $\eta\le\lambda/(2h+2)$ where $\lambda=(d_0/2)^h$ (shrinking $\eta$ only changes $T$), and assume $n$ large (the statement is meant for $n$ larger than some $n_0(\varepsilon,h)$; for tiny $n$ a graph may be $\varepsilon$-far yet too small to contain $H$), so that $c\ge2h/\lambda$.

Put the classes of $H$ into $V_1,V_2,V_3$ respectively and choose images of the $h$ vertices one at a time. For each not-yet-embedded vertex $w$ (class $j$) keep a candidate set $C(w)\subseteq V_j$: the common neighbours of the images already chosen in the other two classes. Initially $C(w)=V_j$. When a vertex $v$ is embedded at $x$, each $C(w)$ with $w$ in another class is replaced by $C(w)\cap N(x)$.

**Claim.** At every step each $|C(w)|\ge\lambda c$ and the vertex $v$ can be embedded in at least $\frac{\lambda}{2}c$ ways. Indeed $|C(v)|\ge\lambda c$. By the Counting lemma, for each of the at most $h$ other candidate sets $C(w)$ (all of size $\ge\lambda c\ge\eta c$) fewer than $\eta c$ vertices $x\in V_j$ fail $|N(x)\cap C(w)|\ge(d_0-\eta)|C(w)|\ge\frac{d_0}2|C(w)|$. Excluding these $<h\eta c$ vertices and the $\le h$ already used ones leaves at least $\lambda c-h\eta c-h\ge\frac\lambda2c$ choices. A good choice shrinks each $C(w)$ by a factor $\ge d_0/2$, and each $C(w)$ shrinks at most $h$ times, so it stays $\ge(d_0/2)^hc=\lambda c$.

Hence the number of ordered embeddings is at least $\big(\tfrac12(d_0/2)^hc\big)^h$ ($h$ distinct choices at each step), and each copy of $H$ is counted at most $h!$ times. With $c\ge\frac{3n}{4T}$ this is at least $\delta(\varepsilon,h)n^h$. ∎

(Counting lemma used below, from the proof of the Coupon theorem: if $(V_i,V_j)$ is $\varepsilon$-regular with density $d\ge\varepsilon$ then all but fewer than $\varepsilon|V_i|$ vertices of $V_i$ have at least $(d-\varepsilon)|Y|$ neighbours in any given $Y\subseteq V_j$ with $|Y|\ge\varepsilon|V_j|$; indeed otherwise those exceptional vertices $X$ would give $d(X,Y)<d-\varepsilon$.)

pumac-2019-power-25.title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits for $\chi=3$
pumac-2019-power-25.body:
**Lower bound.** $K_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil n/2\rceil}$ is bipartite, so $3$-chromatic $H$ is not a subgraph, and it has $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ edges.

**Upper bound.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $G$ a graph on $n$ vertices with more than $(\frac14+\varepsilon)n^2$ edges. If fewer than $\varepsilon n^2$ edges were removed, more than $\frac{n^2}4$ would remain, so by Mantel a triangle would remain. Hence $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far from triangle-free. Let $h=|V(H)|$. By Problem 2.3.1, $G$ contains at least $\delta n^{3h}>0$ copies of $K(h,h,h)$ for $n$ large. Since $\chi(H)=3$, colouring $H$ with three colours gives $H\subseteq K(h,h,h)$. So $G$ contains $H$. Hence for $n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)$, $\mathrm{ex}(n,H)\le(\frac14+\varepsilon)n^2$, which with the lower bound proves the claim. ∎

pumac-2019-power-26a.title: Encoding via regularity
pumac-2019-power-26a.body:
**Lower bound.** Every subgraph of the complete bipartite graph with parts $\{1..\lfloor n/2\rfloor\}$, $\{\ldots\}$ is triangle-free, so $T(n)\ge2^{\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor}$, giving (1) with $a=2$, $c=\frac15$ for $n\ge 2$.

**Upper bound $T(n)\le2^{(1/4+\eta)n^2}$** (for any $\eta>0$ and $n$ large; this implies (2), which is also trivial because $T(n)\le2^{\binom n2}<2^{n^2/2}$).

Given $\eta$ pick $\varepsilon>0$ small and $t=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$, $T_0=T(\varepsilon,t)$. For a triangle-free $G$ take an $\varepsilon$-regular partition $V_0,\dots,V_k$ with $t\le k\le T_0$ (as $n\ge T_0$). Let $G_1$ be $G$ minus all edges meeting $V_0$, inside parts, in irregular pairs, and in pairs of density $<\varepsilon$. As in the Coupon theorem's computation, $G\setminus G_1$ has at most $\varepsilon'n^2$ edges with $\varepsilon'=3\varepsilon+\varepsilon/2$ (at most $\varepsilon n^2$ at $V_0$, $\frac{n^2}{2t}\le\frac\varepsilon2n^2$ inside parts, $\varepsilon n^2$ in irregular pairs, $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}n^2$ in sparse pairs).

Let $R$ be the reduced graph on $\{1,..,k\}$: $ij\in R$ iff $(V_i,V_j)$ is a regular pair of density $\ge\varepsilon$ kept in $G_1$. **$R$ is triangle-free**: a triangle $ijl$ in $R$ with densities $\ge\varepsilon$ would, by the counting argument of the Coupon theorem (applied with regularity parameter $\varepsilon/3$; take $\varepsilon$ small and use a regularity parameter $\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon/3$ in the partition from the start), produce a triangle of $G$. By Mantel, $|R|\le k^2/4$.

**Counting encodings.** The data $(V_0,\dots,V_k)$: at most $(T_0+1)^n$ choices. $R$: at most $2^{T_0^2}$. $G_1$ given $R$: each pair in $R$ has at most $2^{(n/k)^2}$ edge sets, total $\le2^{|R|(n/k)^2}\le2^{n^2/4}$. $G\setminus G_1$: a subset of at most $\varepsilon'n^2$ of the $\binom n2$ pairs: at most $2^{H_2(2\varepsilon')n^2/2}$ choices (binary entropy, valid for $\varepsilon'<\frac14$). Altogether $T(n)\le(T_0+1)^n\,2^{T_0^2}\,2^{n^2/4}\,2^{H_2(2\varepsilon')n^2/2}$. Choosing $\varepsilon$ so small that $H_2(2\varepsilon')/2<\eta/2$ and $n$ large enough that the first two factors are below $2^{\eta n^2/2}$ gives $T(n)\le2^{(1/4+\eta)n^2}$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-26b.title: Squeeze
pumac-2019-power-26b.body:
Subgraphs of the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil n/2\rceil$ are triangle-free, so $\log_2T(n)\ge\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$. By part (a), for every $\eta>0$ and large $n$, $\log_2T(n)\le(\frac14+\eta)n^2$. Therefore $\frac14-o(1)\le\frac{\log_2T(n)}{n^2}\le\frac14+\eta$ for large $n$, so the limit exists and equals $\frac14$.

**Answer: $1/4$**

pumac-2019-power-27.title: Greedy embedding into a regular pair
pumac-2019-power-27.body:
Let $\varepsilon=c^3/1000$ (so $\varepsilon<c/4$), $t=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$, $T=T(\varepsilon,t)$; assume $n\ge T$ (for $n<T$ we have $\delta n<1$, so $H$ is the empty graph and the statement is vacuous). Take an $\varepsilon$-regular partition $V_0,\dots,V_k$, $c'=|V_i|\ge\frac{3n}{4T}$.

**A dense regular pair.** Remove edges at $V_0$ ($\le\varepsilon n^2$), inside parts ($\le\frac{n^2}{2t}\le\varepsilon n^2$), in irregular pairs ($\le\varepsilon n^2$), and in pairs of density $<c/2$ ($\le\frac c4n^2$). Since $3\varepsilon+\frac c4<cn^2/n^2$, at least one edge survives, so some pair $(A,B)=(V_i,V_j)$ is $\varepsilon$-regular with density $d\ge c/2$.

**Embedding.** Let $H$ have bipartition $(P,Q)$, $|H|=h\le\delta n$, max degree $\le3$; we embed $P$ into $A$ and $Q$ into $B$. Order the vertices $v_1,\dots,v_h$ and keep for each not yet embedded $w$ the candidate set $C(w)\subseteq A$ or $B$ (its side), initially all of it. By the Counting lemma, if $|C(w)|\ge\varepsilon c'$, all but $<\varepsilon c'$ vertices $x$ of the opposite side have $|N(x)\cap C(w)|\ge(d-\varepsilon)|C(w)|\ge\frac d2|C(w)|$. When we embed $v$ at $x\in C(v)$ (not used before and typical for each of the at most $3$ unembedded neighbours $w$ of $v$), replace $C(w)$ by $C(w)\cap N(x)$. A vertex has $\le3$ neighbours, so $|C(w)|$ shrinks at most $3$ times, to at least $(d/2)^3c'\ge(c/4)^3c'=\frac{c^3}{64}c'$. Available choices for $v$: $|C(v)|-h-3\varepsilon c'\ge\frac{c^3}{64}c'-\delta n-\frac{3c^3}{1000}c'>0$ provided $\delta n\le\frac{c^3}{128}c'$, which holds for $\delta=\frac{c^3}{128}\cdot\frac{3}{4T}$. Also $|C(w)|\ge\frac{c^3}{64}c'>\varepsilon c'$ throughout. The embedding is edge-preserving: each edge $vw$ of $H$ is placed when the later endpoint is embedded, in the common neighbourhood. After $h$ steps we have a copy of $H$ in $G$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-28.title: Peeling perfect matchings in a regular pair
pumac-2019-power-28.body:
**Dense regular pair.** As in Problem 2.3.4, with regularity parameter $\eta$ small in terms of $\varepsilon$, there is an $\eta$-regular pair $(A,B)$, $|A|=|B|=m\ge\frac{3n}{4T}$, with density $d\ge\varepsilon/2$.

**Trimming.** Let $A'\subseteq A$ be the vertices with at least $(d-\eta)m$ neighbours in $B$ and $B'\subseteq B$ those with $\ge(d-\eta)m$ neighbours in $A$; $|A\setminus A'|,|B\setminus B'|<\eta m$. Cut $A',B'$ to a common size $m'\ge(1-\eta)m$ (delete arbitrary vertices). Let $H_0$ be the bipartite graph induced between them. Each vertex has degree $\ge(d-3\eta)m\ge\frac d2m'$ and for $X\subseteq A'$, $Y\subseteq B'$ with $|X|,|Y|\ge2\eta m'\ (\ge\eta m)$ regularity gives $d(X,Y)\ge d-\eta\ge\frac d2$, so $e_{H_0}(X,Y)\ge\frac d2|X||Y|$.

**Peeling.** Let $r=\lfloor d\eta m'/2\rfloor$ and $\eta\le d/16$. We find $r$ edge-disjoint perfect matchings of $H_0$ one at a time. Let $H_j$ be $H_0$ minus $j<r$ perfect matchings. Then min degree $\ge\frac d2m'-r\ge\frac d4m'\ge4\eta m'$, and for $|X|,|Y|\ge2\eta m'$: $e_{H_j}(X,Y)\ge\frac d2|X||Y|-j\min(|X|,|Y|)>0$ (since $\frac d2\cdot2\eta m'=d\eta m'>r$). Check **Hall's condition** for $X\subseteq A'$:
- $|X|\le4\eta m'$: $|N(X)|\ge$ min degree $\ge4\eta m'\ge|X|$.
- $4\eta m'<|X|\le(1-2\eta)m'$: if $|N(X)|<m'-2\eta m'$ then $Y=B'\setminus N(X)$ has $|Y|>2\eta m'$ and no edge to $X$, contradicting $e(X,Y)>0$. So $|N(X)|\ge(1-2\eta)m'\ge|X|$.
- $|X|>(1-2\eta)m'$: every $b\in B'$ has $\ge4\eta m'>|A'\setminus X|$ neighbours, so $N(X)=B'$.

Hence $H_j$ has a perfect matching. The union of the $r$ matchings is an $r$-regular bipartite subgraph of $G$ with $r\ge d\eta m'/4\ge\frac{\varepsilon\eta}{8}\cdot\frac{3n}{4T}\cdot\frac12\ge\delta n$ for a suitable $\delta(\varepsilon)>0$. ∎

*Interpretation.* 'Regular subgraph' is understood as in the official solution: a subgraph (not necessarily induced) in which every selected vertex has degree exactly $k$.

pumac-2019-power-29.title: Isomorphism invariance; counterexample
pumac-2019-power-29.body:
**Isomorphic:** let $\sigma:V(G)\to V(H)$ be an isomorphism. If $H$ could be turned into some $H'\in P$ by $<\varepsilon n^2$ edge changes, then applying $\sigma^{-1}$ to the same changes turns $G$ into $\sigma^{-1}(H')$, which is isomorphic to $H'$ and so in $P$ (closure under isomorphism), with the same number of changes: contradiction.

**Homomorphic:** No. Take $P$ = 'has no edges', $G=K_n$ and $H$ the graph on $n$ vertices with no edges. There is a homomorphism $H\to G$ (the identity map; no edge needs to be preserved). $G$ is $\frac1{2}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n}$-far from $P$ (all $\binom n2$ edges must be deleted), while $H\in P$ is $0$-far.

**Answer: yes for isomorphic graphs; no for merely homomorphic ones.**

pumac-2019-power-30.title: Each property
pumac-2019-power-30.body:
For $n\le n_0(\varepsilon)$ the tester may query all $\binom n2$ pairs (a bounded number), so assume $n$ is large.

(i) **Connected.** Any graph on $n$ vertices becomes connected after adding at most $n-1<\varepsilon n^2$ edges ($n>1/\varepsilon$), so no graph is $\varepsilon$-far; the tester that always accepts works (zero queries).

(ii) **Has a cycle.** Adding at most $3$ edges to any graph with $n\ge3$ vertices creates a triangle; $3<\varepsilon n^2$ for large $n$, so again always accept.

(iii) **Contains a $k$-clique.** Adding at most $\binom k2$ edges among $k$ vertices creates a $k$-clique, and $\binom k2<\varepsilon n^2$ for large $n$: always accept.

(iv) **Vertex of degree $n-1$.** Joining a vertex to all others needs at most $n-1<\varepsilon n^2$ additions: always accept.

(v) **3-colorable.** Tester: choose $100/\varepsilon^2$ vertices uniformly at random, query all $\binom{100/\varepsilon^2}{2}$ pairs among them (a number depending only on $\varepsilon$), and accept iff the induced subgraph is $3$-colorable. If $G$ is $3$-colorable every induced subgraph is, so it accepts with probability $1$. If $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far, the Theorem says the sample is not $3$-colorable with high probability (more than $0.9$ after the standard repetition remark), so it rejects. Hence all five properties are testable. ∎

pumac-2019-power-31.title: Sampling triples
pumac-2019-power-31.body:
Let $\delta=\delta(\varepsilon)$ from the Coupon theorem and $m=\lceil\frac{\ln 10}{6\delta}\rceil+1$. Tester: choose $m$ independent uniformly random $3$-element vertex sets, query the three pairs of each ($3m$ queries, independent of $n$), reject iff some chosen triple is a triangle.

If $G$ is triangle-free, it is never rejected (one-sided). If $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far from triangle-free it has $\ge\delta n^3\ge6\delta\binom n3$ triangles, so each sampled triple is a triangle with probability $\ge6\delta$, and the probability that none of the $m$ triples is a triangle is at most $(1-6\delta)^m\le e^{-6\delta m}\le\frac1{10}$. So the tester rejects with probability $\ge0.9$ (take $m$ slightly larger for strict inequality). ∎

pumac-2019-power-32.title: Homomorphism counting
pumac-2019-power-32.body:
The average degree is $\bar d\ge2\varepsilon n$. Homomorphisms $K_{1,j}\to G$ (a centre and $j$ ordered neighbours) number $\sum_vd(v)^j\ge n\bar d^{\,j}\ge n(2\varepsilon n)^j$ by Jensen (convexity of $x^j$).

Homomorphisms $K_{s,t}\to G$ are tuples $(v_1,\dots,v_s;w_1,\dots,w_t)$ with every $v_i\sim w_j$; their number is $\sum_{(v_1..v_s)}|N(v_1)\cap\dots\cap N(v_s)|^t$. By Jensen over the $n^s$ tuples this is at least $n^s\,\mu^t$ where $\mu=n^{-s}\sum_{(v_i)}|\bigcap N(v_i)|=n^{-s}\sum_wd(w)^s\ge n^{-s}\,n(2\varepsilon n)^s=n(2\varepsilon)^s$. So there are at least $(2\varepsilon)^{st}n^{s+t}$ homomorphisms.

A homomorphism is non-injective only if two of the $v_i$ coincide or two of the $w_j$ coincide (a $v_i$ can't equal a $w_j$ since they are adjacent); there are at most $\binom{s+t}2n^{s+t-1}$ of those. So at least $(1-o(1))(2\varepsilon)^{st}n^{s+t}$ injective homomorphisms, i.e. the random $(s+t)$-tuple spans $K_{s,t}$ with probability $\ge(1-o(1))(2\varepsilon)^{st}$ (the denominator $n(n-1)\cdots$ is $\le n^{s+t}$).

**General bipartite $H$.** Let $H$ have classes of sizes $s,t$ ($s+t=h$, so $st\le h^2/4$); then $H\subseteq K_{s,t}$ on the same vertex set. Every injective homomorphism $K_{s,t}\to G$ restricts to an injective homomorphism $H\to G$, and each copy of $H$ in $G$ arises from at most $h!$ of them. So the number of copies is at least $\frac{1}{h!}(1-o(1))(2\varepsilon)^{st}n^h\ge c(H)\varepsilon^{h^2/4}n^h$ (as $\varepsilon\le1$, $(2\varepsilon)^{st}\ge\varepsilon^{st}\ge\varepsilon^{h^2/4}$), with $c(H)=\frac1{2h!}$ and $n(H)$ large enough that the $(1-o(1))\ge\frac12$ and the floor is harmless. ∎

pumac-2019-power-33.title: Construction
pumac-2019-power-33.body:
Let $m$ be a parameter and $X$ as in the Lemma. Let $G_0$ be the $5$-partite graph with classes $W_1,\dots,W_5$ (disjoint copies of $[im]$, i.e. $W_i=\{1,\dots,im\}$), where for $a\in W_i$, $b\in W_{i+1}$ ($i=1..4$): $a\sim b$ iff $b-a\in X$; and for $a\in W_1,b\in W_5$: $a\sim b$ iff $b-a\in4X$.

**Designed cycles.** For $j\in[m]$, $x\in X$, the vertices $j\in W_1,j+x\in W_2,\dots,j+4x\in W_5$ form a $C_5$. There are $m|X|$ of them and they are edge-disjoint: an edge between $W_i,W_{i+1}$ (or $W_5,W_1$) determines $x$ and $j$.

**No other $5$-cycles.** Edges only join $W_i,W_{i+1}$ (indices mod $5$), so a $5$-cycle takes one vertex $v_i$ from each class, $v_{i+1}-v_i=x_i\in X$ ($i\le4$) and $v_5-v_1=4x_5$ with $x_5\in X$. Then $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=4x_5$, so all $x_i$ coincide by the Lemma and the cycle is a designed one. So $G_0$ has exactly $m|X|$ copies of $C_5$ and every edge is in exactly one.

**Blow-up.** Let $r=\lfloor n/(15m)\rfloor$ (so $n\ge15mr$) and $G$ be the $r$-blow-up of $G_0$ ($|V(G_0)|=15m$) plus $n-15mr<15m$ isolated vertices. A $5$-cycle in $G$ maps homomorphically to a closed walk of length $5$ in $G_0$; since each step moves $W_i\to W_{i\pm1}$ and $5$ steps must return, all steps go the same way, so it projects to a $5$-cycle of $G_0$. Thus $G$ contains exactly $m|X|r^5$ copies of $C_5$, and each edge of $G$ (a blown-up edge) lies in exactly $r^3$ of them. Destroying all of them needs at least $\frac{m|X|r^5}{r^3}=m|X|r^2$ edge deletions. As $n\le30mr$ (for $r\ge1$), $\frac{m|X|r^2}{n^2}\ge\frac{|X|}{900m}\ge\frac{1}{900\cdot2^{10\sqrt{\log m}}}=:\varepsilon_m$, so $G$ is $\varepsilon_m$-far from $C_5$-free. The number of copies is $m|X|r^5\le m^2\big(\frac n{15m}\big)^5\le\frac{n^5}{m^3}$.

**Parameters.** Given small $\varepsilon$ let $m$ be the largest integer with $900\cdot2^{10\sqrt{\log m}}\le1/\varepsilon$ (so $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_m$, hence $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far). Maximality gives $900\cdot2^{10\sqrt{\log(m+1)}}>1/\varepsilon$, i.e. $\log(m+1)>\frac1{100}\log^2\frac1{900\varepsilon}\ge\frac1{400}\log^2\frac1\varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon$, so $m+1\ge\varepsilon^{-\frac1{400}\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ and, as $m\ge(m+1)/2$, $\frac1{m^3}\le\frac{8}{(m+1)^3}\le8\varepsilon^{\frac3{400}\log(1/\varepsilon)}\le\varepsilon^{c\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ with $c=\frac1{200}$ for small $\varepsilon$. Hence $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far from $C_5$-free and has at most $\varepsilon^{c\log(1/\varepsilon)}n^5$ copies of $C_5$ (for $n$ large enough that $r\ge1$). ∎

pumac-2019-power-34.title: Both directions
pumac-2019-power-34.body:
**Bipartite $\Rightarrow$ easily testable.** If $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far from $H$-free, deleting all edges would give an $H$-free graph, so $G$ has at least $\varepsilon n^2$ edges. By (A) it has $\ge c(H)\varepsilon^{h^2/4}n^h$ copies of $H$, so a uniformly random $h$-set of vertices contains a copy with probability $\ge p_0=c(H)\varepsilon^{h^2/4}h!/\!\!$ (at least $c'\varepsilon^{h^2/4}$, since $n^h/\binom nh\ge h!$). Tester: for $q=\lceil\frac{3}{p_0}\rceil$ independent random $h$-sets query all $\binom h2$ pairs each, and reject iff a copy of $H$ is found. If $G$ is $H$-free it is never rejected; if $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far it is rejected with probability $\ge1-(1-p_0)^q\ge1-e^{-3}>0.9$. The number of queries is $q\binom h2=O_H(\varepsilon^{-h^2/4})$, polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ (for $n\le n(H)$ query everything, a constant number).

**Non-bipartite $\Rightarrow$ not easily testable.** A tester that makes $Q$ queries sees at most $2Q$ vertices, and (after randomly relabelling the vertices of the input, which does not change the problem) its view is a labelled induced subgraph on at most $y=2Q$ random vertices, with its decision made from that view. Take $G$ from (B): $\varepsilon$-far from $H$-free with fewer than $\varepsilon^{c_H\log(1/\varepsilon)}n^h$ copies of $H$. A random set of $y$ vertices contains a copy of $H$ with probability at most $\#\text{copies}\cdot\binom{y}{h}/\binom nh\le\varepsilon^{c_H\log(1/\varepsilon)}\,y^h\cdot O(1)$. To make the tester reject $G$ with probability $>0.9$ while its view contains no copy of $H$ (and hence looks like a view of an $H$-free graph) it must see a copy of $H$ with constant probability, so $y^h\gtrsim\varepsilon^{-c_H\log(1/\varepsilon)}$, i.e. $Q\ge\varepsilon^{-\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))}$, which is super-polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$. ∎

pumac-2019-power-35.title: Twins versus independent graphs
pumac-2019-power-35.body:
Let $P$ be the property: $V=V_1\cup V_2$, $|V_1|=|V_2|=n/2$, no edges between $V_1,V_2$, and $G[V_1]\cong G[V_2]$.

Two distributions on $n$-vertex graphs (vertex set $[n]$, with a uniformly random labelling):
- $\mathcal D_1$: take a random graph $R\sim G(n/2,\frac12)$, put two copies of $R$ on two halves (with the copies matched by a bijection, 'twin' vertices), and randomly relabel. Always in $P$.
- $\mathcal D_2$: put independent random graphs $R_1,R_2\sim G(n/2,\frac12)$ on the two halves and randomly relabel.

**$\mathcal D_2$ is far from $P$ with high probability.** For a fixed split of $V$ into halves and a fixed bijection $\phi$ between them, the number of pairs on which $R_1$ and $\phi^{-1}R_2$ disagree is $\mathrm{Bin}(\binom{n/2}2,\frac12)$; the probability it is below $\frac{1}{4}\binom{n/2}2$ is $\le e^{-cn^2}$. There are at most $2^n\cdot(n/2)!=e^{O(n\log n)}$ choices of (split, bijection). So w.h.p. every split and bijection leaves at least $\frac14\binom{n/2}{2}\approx n^2/32$ disagreements, and any graph in $P$ differs from $G$ in at least $\frac12$ of that (to reach $P$ one must fix the disagreements on one half or cross edges): $G$ is $\varepsilon_0$-far from $P$ for a constant $\varepsilon_0$ (say $\varepsilon_0=1/100$) with probability $1-o(1)$.

**Views coincide.** Suppose a tester makes $Q$ queries and touches at most $2Q$ vertices. When the tester queries a pair $(u,v)$, an adjacency bit in $\mathcal D_1$ is an independent fair bit unless a queried vertex is the twin of an earlier queried vertex (then the bit repeats an earlier one); in $\mathcal D_2$ every queried pair gives a fresh fair bit. By random labelling, each newly touched vertex is a twin of one of the previously touched ones with probability $\le\frac{2Q}{n-1}$, so the probability that any twin collision happens is $\le\frac{4Q^2}{n-1}$. Without a collision the answer sequences have identical distribution. Hence the acceptance probabilities differ by at most $\frac{4Q^2}{n-1}$.

**Conclusion.** A tester must accept $\mathcal D_1$ with probability $>0.9$. If $Q\le c\sqrt n$ with $c$ small, it accepts $\mathcal D_2$ with probability $>0.5$, so averaging over $\mathcal D_2$ (which is far from $P$ w.h.p.) there exists a graph $\varepsilon_0$-far from $P$ that is accepted with probability $>0.1$, violating the rejection requirement. Hence every $\varepsilon_0$-tester needs $Q\ge c\sqrt n$ queries, unbounded in $n$: $P$ is not testable. ∎

pumac-2019-power-36.title: Reduced graphs
pumac-2019-power-36.body:
Fix $\delta$, put $\varepsilon_0=\delta/10$ small enough for the counting lemma (in terms of $\delta,h=|H|$), $k\le T=T(\varepsilon_0,\lceil1/\varepsilon_0\rceil)$, and densities taken from the grid $\{0,\varepsilon_0,2\varepsilon_0,\dots\}$. Let $\mathcal R$ be the family of all regularity-instances $R=(\varepsilon_0,k,(\eta_{ij}),\bar R)$ with $k\le T$ whose **reduced graph** $F_R$ (vertices $1..k$, $ij$ an edge iff $\eta_{ij}\ge\delta/2$, $i\ne j$) has no homomorphic image of $H$ (i.e. there is no homomorphism $H\to F_R$). There are boundedly many such instances: $r=r(\delta)$.

**(2).** Let $G'$ satisfy some $R\in\mathcal R$. Delete from $G'$ the edges at exceptional pairs ($\bar R$ and irregular ones, $\le\varepsilon_0n^2$), inside parts ($\le n^2/(2k)\le\varepsilon_0n^2$) and in pairs with $\eta_{ij}<\delta/2$ ($\le\frac\delta4n^2$). The remaining graph has no copy of $H$: a copy would put its vertices into parts, giving a homomorphism $H\to F_R$ (all edges used lie in regular pairs of density $\ge\delta/2$) — and conversely the counting lemma is not needed for this direction. So $G'$ is $<\delta n^2$ close to $H$-free. If $G$ is $\varepsilon$-far from $H$-free and $G'$ satisfies $R$, then $\mathrm{dist}(G,P)\le\mathrm{dist}(G,G')+\mathrm{dist}(G',P)$ gives $\mathrm{dist}(G,G')\ge(\varepsilon-\delta)n^2$. So $G$ is $(\varepsilon-\delta)$-far from satisfying $R$.

**(1).** Let $G$ be $H$-free. Take an $\varepsilon_0$-regular equipartition with $k\le T$ parts and let $\eta_{ij}$ be the density of $(V_i,V_j)$ rounded down to the grid, $\bar R$ the irregular pairs. The reduced graph $F$ (edges: regular pairs of density $\ge\delta/2$) has no homomorphic image of $H$, since otherwise the counting lemma would produce a copy of $H$ in $G$. Changing each regular pair's density to $\eta_{ij}$ (by removing or adding $\le\varepsilon_0|V_i||V_j|$ random edges, which preserves $2\varepsilon_0$-regularity with high probability) and treating the $\le\varepsilon_0n$ vertices of any exceptional part as a part, costs $<\delta n^2$ changes; the resulting graph satisfies the instance $R\in\mathcal R$ (up to a harmless adjustment of $\varepsilon_0$). So $G$ is $\delta$-close to satisfying $R$. ∎

(The verification that random edge changes preserve regularity is routine and only sketched here, as in the official solution.)
